title: Tinker and the Wobbly Bridge
markdown:
Way out in Whispering Woods lived a termite named Tinker. The trees whispered secrets to the wind, and the flowers giggled when you tickled them. Tinker was a super special termite. He could design the most amazing twisty-turny tunnels under the ground. His little termite palaces were the talk of the forest floor. He could make tunnels so twisty and turny they would make your head spin, in a fun way. But oh, Tinker was very afraid of one thing: things that were up.

Just looking up at a tall mushroom made his tiny feelers quiver and his little legs shake. And a wobbly leaning bridge? That was like a nightmare.

This year the bridge was a big problem. It was the bridge the grand Woodland Parade always used. Imagine it. Bunnies hopping in sparkly vests, squirrels balancing acorn hats, and old Mr. Badger with his wheezy accordion. Oh, the joyful noise. But this year the bridge was leaning. It was tilting. It looked as if it had had too much fizzy berry juice and was about to take a nap.

Tinker stood near the edge. A wobble started in his tummy, but it was not the bridge. It was his fear doing a little jig. He looked up, up, up at the sky. The world began to spin like a dizzy dandelion seed. "Oh, fiddlesticks." His voice was just a whisper. "The parade. It is coming today. And this bridge looks as if it might do a splat." He could almost hear the crackle of breaking wood. A shiver ran all the way down his little termite tail. His insides felt as if they were made of jelly.

Just then, stomp, stomp, stomp. Who came striding along? It was Maple the moose. Maple was enormous, as tall as three picnic tables stacked up high. Her eyes were as soft and kind as moss on a sunny rock. She saw Tinker quivering near the edge of the wobbly bridge, his tiny jaws chattering like little nervous castanets.

"Oh, hello, Tinker." Her voice was as warm and comforting as a mug of hot chocolate on a chilly day. "What has got you looking so wobbly yourself?"

Tinker pointed a shaky leg. His whole body was trembling. "Maple. The bridge. It is leaning. And the parade. Oh, the parade will never get across. It is going to be a disaster." He was practically vibrating with worry. His insides felt as if they were doing a trampoline act, all bouncy and wobbly when he just wanted them to be still.

Maple lowered her big gentle head, her antlers brushing the leaves of a nearby fern. She looked at the bridge. "You are right, Tinker. It is leaning quite a bit. And the parade needs this bridge to be safe. It is a very important bridge, indeed." She looked at Tinker, her kind eyes full of understanding. "You are such a clever builder, Tinker. You know more about wood than anyone. Do you think you could help me fix it?"

Tinker gulped. Help? Fix the bridge? The high, wobbly bridge? He tried to be brave. He scampered onto the very edge of the bridge, which felt like climbing the tallest tree in the forest. He saw a small loose twig. "Okay. I can do this." He puffed out his tiny chest. He nudged the twig with all his strength. Wobble, wobble. The twig just rolled right off the side and disappeared into the ferns below. Plink. Tinker felt his bravery deflate like a leaky balloon. "Oh, dear. That did not help at all. I am just too small, Maple. And too scared of heights." A tear prickled his eye.

Maple nudged him gently with her soft nose, a gesture as comforting as a warm hug. "Do not say that, Tinker. Even the smallest builders can do mighty things. And you are not alone. I am here." She looked around, her brow furrowed in thought. "You are the expert on wood, Tinker. You know how to make things strong. And I am strong, and I can reach the higher bits and hold things steady." She smiled, a warm wide smile. "Maybe we just need to think about what you can do, not what you cannot." She chuckled, a rumble in her chest. "Besides, I cannot exactly fit into your super-secret underground tunnels, can I? But you can."

Just then a big gust of wind swept through the woods, rustling the leaves like a thousand tiny dancers. The bridge swayed. Then snap. A small important-looking piece of wood cracked off and tumbled down into the bushes. "Oh no," cried Tinker. His fear came rushing back, bigger and stronger than ever. He wanted to burrow deep, deep, deep underground and never, ever come out.

But then he looked at Maple. She was standing there, calm and steady, even though the wind was tugging at her fur. She had not run away. She was still looking at the bridge, her big eyes thoughtful. And Tinker remembered her words. What you can do. He looked at the broken piece, then down at the sturdy oak tree roots that held up one side of the bridge. He knew those roots. He knew how to make things safe underground. He knew how to build.

"Maple." A brand new idea buzzed in his tiny head like a happy bee. "I cannot reach up high, but I can work underneath. I can tunnel into the ground and build supports from below. I can shore up the foundation. I can gnaw new little wooden pegs to hold things together where they broke." He was practically shouting now, his fear forgotten. A fizzy exciting energy took its place.

Maple’s eyes lit up like fireflies on a summer night. "That is brilliant, Tinker. Absolutely brilliant. You be my underground engineer, and I will be your ground-level sturdy-holder."

So off Tinker went, scritch-scratch, scritch-scratch. His sharp mandibles worked away like tiny busy shovels, burrowing into the rich dark soil beneath the bridge. He dug and he tunnelled, creating strong new foundations, like building strong legs for the bridge. He gnawed perfect little wooden pegs, sharp and smooth. Meanwhile Maple carefully held the wobbly bits steady with her strong nose and front legs. Her big body was a shield against any further wobbles. When Tinker popped up from a tunnel to hand her a perfectly shaped peg, she carefully, ever so carefully, put it into place.

They worked and they worked. The sun climbed higher and higher, painting the woods in golden light. Tinker’s fear of heights was still there, a little flutter in his tummy, but he was too busy being a super-duper builder to let it stop him. He was making the bridge strong, from the roots all the way up.

Finally, with a last strong push from Maple and a final perfect peg from Tinker, the bridge settled. It was not leaning anymore. It was straight and sturdy and looked as safe as a cozy burrow.

Just then they heard it. Toot. Toot. Clomp, clomp. The Woodland Parade was coming. And as the first bunny hopped onto the bridge, followed by the squirrels, and then old Mr. Badger with his accordion, who gave a little grumpy nod of approval, Tinker watched from the safety of the ground. His chest was puffed out with pride. He had been scared, yes, but he had also been brave. He had helped. He and Maple had saved the parade.

And as the joyful music and happy chatter of the parade echoed through the Whispering Woods, Tinker the termite felt a happy proud wobble in his tummy that had nothing to do with heights. It was the best kind of wobble.
